resources.string: The guide
Back

Tempo shows the time, the date and your day in one view, read from the calendars your phone already has. This guide walks through Today, the month and the widgets, says what each part answers, and points out the things worth knowing that a screen cannot say out loud.
Where your events come from

Tempo reads the phone’s own calendar: every account the phone already syncs, Google, Samsung, Exchange or the phone’s own calendar, is there. There is nothing to sign in to and nothing for Tempo to sync: what your calendar app has, Tempo shows.
Your calendars, your choice

In the settings every calendar has a switch, grouped by account and with its colour. One you never chose for is shown as your calendar app shows it; a choice you make stays with that calendar, even if it is renamed.
All-day events keep their date

A birthday or a holiday is stored as a date, not as a time, and Tempo reads it that way: it stays on its own day wherever you are, and a trip across time zones never moves it to the day before. An event that runs for days says which day of it this is.
Declined and cancelled
A cancelled event is never shown. An invitation you declined is left out too, unless you turn it on in the settings, where it is struck through.
Work calendars
Android keeps a work profile’s calendars apart from the personal ones, on purpose. To see them, install Tempo in the work profile as well: there it reads the work calendars.
Today
The time large, the date above it, and one sentence before any list: the event under way and when it ends, the next one and how soon, or how long you are free.
An example clock face at twenty past ten, with a meeting under way until eleven and two more events later in the day
An example: twenty past ten, a meeting under way until eleven in the accent, two more events later in the day, each in its calendar’s colour.
The dial

Beside the time, while today has something left, a clock face with it on its ring: what comes next in the accent, the rest quieter, each in its calendar’s colour. The hour hand walks through a meeting as it goes. The ring holds the next twelve hours, less half an hour: an event that goes on beyond them fades out at that end, and early in the day an afternoon’s events wait off the ring until they are within reach. Another day’s events are in the list, not on the face, and with nothing left today the face is not drawn. It is the face of the «At a glance» widget.
The date and the time

Each opens the app it belongs to: a touch on the date, your calendar app on today; a touch on the time, its figures or its clock face, the phone’s Clock app, where the alarms and the timers are. A switch in the settings turns the time’s touch off. Scroll down the day and a bar keeps the two at the top of the page, with the month’s and the settings’ buttons, each opening what it opens above.
The day in order

Today’s events one under the other, each with its calendar’s colour as a mark. The one under way stands out on a ground in the accent and says how long is left; with nothing under way, a line marks now. The ones that are over grow quieter, and two or more of them fold into one line that opens.
Free time

Your next free hour or more today is a row of its own, where it falls: a touch on it starts a new event there, and the sentence says how long you are free. Shorter gaps, and the free time later on, are left out, so the day does not fill up with rows of free time.
The days ahead
Tomorrow and the days after it, each under its name with a short summary; a run of empty days is said once. In the settings: two weeks, a week, today and tomorrow, or today alone.
The next alarm

The next alarm you set in the Clock app, under the sentence; a touch on it opens the Clock app. Tempo only reads it; a switch in the settings hides it. Some calendar apps keep their reminders as alarms: those are not shown, and an alarm of yours that comes after one appears once the reminder has rung.
Other time zones

An event written in a time zone whose clock reads another time says when it starts there too: “08:00 in Lisbon”. In the settings you can choose a city for a second clock, under the alarm: “New York 04:20”, with “tomorrow” or “yesterday” when its date is not yours. A widget shows it too where you turn it on in its own settings.
On a large screen

On a tablet, or a foldable opened wide, Today stands in two parts: the clock on one side, the day beside it, each scrolling on its own. Under the clock is the current month, with the marks of the month’s own page: a touch on a date opens the month on that day, a touch on its name opens it on today.
Live while you look
While Today is open the clock moves at each minute, and an event made or changed in your calendar app is there when you come back. Once you leave, nothing runs.
The month
From the button beside the settings on Today: a whole month at a glance, to see which days are taken and to plan one. It reads the same calendars as Today, with the same choices.
Marks, not titles

Under each date, what it holds. A dot is an event with a time, in its calendar’s colour: up to three, and a small plus when there are more. A bar is an event that takes whole days, a birthday, a holiday, a trip: it runs across the days it covers, so a week away reads as a week. Days gone by are drawn quieter, and so are the few days of the months beside that complete a week.
The day under the month

A touch on a date lists that day under the month, as Today would: its all-day events, then its events in order, each a touch from your calendar app. The button at the bottom starts a new event on that day; so does a long touch on a date.
Near and far

The months turn under your finger. A touch on the month’s name goes to any month of any year; the small calendar with today’s number on it brings you back, and is there only while you are somewhere else.
A month, and nothing else
There is no week view and no day view here: Today is the day, and the rest is your calendar app’s to draw.
Your calendar app does the writing
Tempo reads your calendar and never writes it. Whatever changes an event happens in your calendar app, which Tempo opens at the right place.
An event
Your calendar app opens it, that very occurrence of it, and changing or deleting it is one step away there.
A new event

From the button at the bottom of Today, from a free row, from the month on the day you chose, or from “New event” on a long press on Tempo’s icon: your calendar app’s new event, its start already set, at the next half hour or where the free time begins. Back in Tempo, it is brought into view, its row glowing for a moment.
A day
The date at the top of Today and a day’s name, on Today and under the month, open your calendar app on that day: for the week, and for whatever else is your calendar app’s to draw.
Alarms and reminders
Alarms are the Clock app’s and reminders your calendar app’s. Tempo sends no notification of its own, so nothing reminds you twice.
On the home screen
Two widgets

«At a glance» is the dial, with what comes next and the day in a few words; «Agenda» puts the time and the date over the rest of your day. Both fit any size, from a single cell up. On a tall «At a glance», the next one or two events under the words; on a wide «Agenda», under the date, how many events are left today and until when. Touch and hold a widget for its own settings: the time and the date, what a touch opens, its colour and opacity.
Never a list to scroll
A card shows as many events as fit whole, laid out for the size it really has, and says how many more there are: nothing is cut in half, nothing scrolls.
Clock times, not countdowns

A card says the time an event starts, never how many minutes away it is: it is redrawn when your calendar changes and when an event starts or ends, not every minute, so a countdown would soon be wrong. Its clock and date are drawn by Android itself, right to the minute, at no cost.
Battery

Tempo has no service and nothing on a timer. With the screen off it does nothing, except when your calendar itself changes, or when an event on a card starts or ends: then it reads the calendar once and redraws, with an alarm that waits for the phone to wake rather than waking it.
Your data

Tempo has no internet permission at all: it sends nothing, to anyone. It keeps no copy of your events: it reads them from the calendar each time, and they stay your calendar’s, travelling with its account or its own backup.

What Tempo keeps is your choices: the formats, the calendars you hide, the appearance. If the phone’s backup is on, Android includes them in it, as it does for other apps: that copy is Android’s, not Tempo’s.
